extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers of philosophy of science, probability, and scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and principles for using probability and experience to infer causes, predict repetition of events, and judge what counts as proof in the domain of perception; includes philosophical remarks on space and time as modes of perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific definition of cause
rubrics_metrics.description: Cause is scientifically used to denote an antecedent stage in a routine of perceptions. In this sense force as a cause is meaningless. First Cause is only a limit, permanent or temporary, to knowledge. No instance, certainly not will, occurs in our experience of an arbitrary first cause in the popular sense of the word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'cause' to refer to antecedent stages within observable routines of perception; do not invoke 'force' or metaphysical first causes as scientific explanations. Treat 'First Cause' claims as statements about the limits of knowledge rather than empirical hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: No inherent necessity in perceptual routine
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no inherent necessity in the routine of perceptions, but the permanent existence of rational beings necessitates a routine of perceptions; with the cessation of routine ceases the possibility of a thinking being. The only necessity we are acquainted with exists in the sphere of conceptions; possibly routine in perceptions is due to the constitution of the perceptive faculty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating claims that posit necessary laws of perception or nature, recognize that such 'necessity' may be a feature of our perceptive faculties or conceptual schemes rather than an absolute property of an unknowable beyond of sense-impression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof in the field of perceptions = overwhelming probability
rubrics_metrics.description: Proof in the field of perceptions is the demonstration of overwhelming probability. Logically we ought to use the word 'know' only of conceptions, and reserve the word 'believe' for perceptions. 'I know that the angle at the circumference on any diameter of a circle is right,' but 'I believe that the sun will rise to-morrow.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat empirical perceptual claims as matters of belief justified by high probability rather than absolute knowledge. Use probabilistic demonstration (very high odds) as the standard of proof for perceptual assertions; be precise in language ('know' vs 'believe').

rubrics_metrics.name: Laplace's principle for updating probabilities
rubrics_metrics.description: "If a result might flow from any one of a certain number of different constitutions, all equally probable before experience, then the several probabilities of each constitution after experience being the real constitution, are proportional to the probabilities that the result would flow from each of these constitutions."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply Laplace's proportional-update principle when you have mutually exclusive hypotheses equally probable a priori; compute posterior odds proportional to the likelihoods each hypothesis would produce the observed result (illustrated by coin/constitution example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equal distribution of ignorance (uniform prior) justified by experience
rubrics_metrics.description: The assumption that any probability-constant about which we know nothing in particular is as likely to have one value as another is grounded upon the rough but solid experience that such constants as a matter of fact as often have one value as another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When adopting a uniform prior (equal distribution of ignorance), justify it by appeal to empirical/statistical experience (Edgeworth example). Recognize critics (e.g., Boole) who question drawing knowledge from complete ignorance and address whether repeated empirical sampling supports the uniform assumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution: ensure identical causes/components before predicting repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: We must be cautious in applying the formula to take a sufficiently comprehensive sequence of perceptions. We must see that the causes are really the same before we predict on the basis of past experience of routine a repetition of sequence in any particular case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before generalizing from repeated observations, verify that the relevant causal components (conditions, season, external factors) are the same; supplement simple repetition counts with contextually relevant observations (example: river floods—consider season, snowmelt, bank conditions). See Mill's Canons for deeper treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining past sequences to assess probability of new sequence
rubrics_metrics.description: If we have experienced m sequences of perceptions which have repeated themselves n times without any anomy, and a new sequence repeated itself r times without anomy, then the odds in favour of the new sequence following routine on the next occasion are m(n−1)+r to 1; if m and n are very great, there will be overwhelming odds in favour of the new sequence following routine although r may be small.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use aggregated past experience across many sequences to raise the probability assigned to a newly observed repeated sequence. This gives quantitative guidance for estimating odds, but requires care about the comparability of sequences (see caution above).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit on probabilistic inference for infinite futures
rubrics_metrics.description: We cannot, however, argue from this result for an infinite future of repetition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the logical limitation: overwhelming probability for any finite interval does not justify claims about infinite repetition. Avoid extrapolating finite-probability results to assertions about the infinite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Space is a mode/order of perceiving coexisting phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Space is a mental expression for the fact that the perceptive faculty has separated coexisting sense-impressions into groups of associated impressions. Space is an order or mode of perceiving objects, but it has no existence if objects are withdrawn, no more than the alphabet could have an existence if there were no letters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing claims about spatial magnitude or spatial facts, treat 'space' as a way we order coexisting perceptions rather than an independently existing container. Use the alphabet analogy to distinguish between objects (sense-impressions) and the order (space).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid emotional/misleading uses of 'infinite space'—contextualize 'how big is space?'
rubrics_metrics.description: 'How big is space?' is a meaningless question as it stands. 'How big is space for me?' admits of an answer: it is just so large as will suffice to separate all things which coexist for me. The author criticizes emotional science that revels in contrasting infinities of space with finite capacities of man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious of rhetorical or emotive appeals about the magnitude or infinity of space; demand precise, contextualized questions and avoid treating perceptual modes as facts about an unknowable beyond. Evaluate astronomical or cosmological claims in terms of perceptual/contextual meaning rather than metaphysical awe.
